# Appendix > **Context:** Key Recommendations + reference appendices for the 2024 Malaysian Management of ED CPG. Includes the diagnosis/treatment algorithm, cardiovascular-disease classification (Princeton consensus), history-taking template, IIEF-5 and EHS questionnaires, PDE5i dosing/contraindications, and procedural references (VED, low-intensity shockwave, penile prosthesis). The Key Recommendations are a consolidated digest — full clinical rationale is in Sections 2–8. ## Key Recommendations The following recommendations are highlighted by the CPG DG as the key recommendations that answer the main questions addressed in the CPG and should be prioritised for implementation. Diagnosis And Assessment: * A comprehensive medical, psychosocial and sexual history should be taken in every patient presenting with erectile dysfunction (ED). * A validated questionnaire related to ED should be used to assess all sexual function domains (e.g. International Index of Erectile Function). * A focused physical examination in the initial assessment of men with ED should be done to identify underlying medical conditions and co-morbid genital disorders that may be associated with ED. * Routine laboratory tests should be performed to identify modifiable risk factors of ED. * Patients with ED should have cardiac risk assessment and vice versa. Treatment: * All patients with erectile dysfunction (ED) should be advised on lifestyle and risk factor modifications. * Phosphodiesterase-5-inhibitor should be offered to all patients with ED unless contraindicated. * Mechanical devices (e.g. using vacuum erection device or shockwave therapy) may be offered in ED. Low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy should be performed by urologists for mild to moderate ED. * Penile prothesis may be offered to patients with ED who have failed other interventions. * An integrated and collaborative approach with psychological interventions should be considered in the treatment of ED. ## Algorithm 1: Diagnosis And Treatment Of ED Overview: This algorithm outlines the complete clinical decision pathway for diagnosing and treating Erectile Dysfunction (ED), from initial patient presentation through to specific treatment selection. The pathway branches based on the type of ED identified (organic or psychogenic) and, for organic ED, further branches based on severity as determined by the IIEF-5 score. **Clinical Definitions And Scoring Reference** IIEF-5 (International Index of Erectile Function, 5-item version) is the validated scoring tool used to assess erectile function and classify severity. The total score is the sum of the ordinal responses to all 5 questions (range: 5 to 25). | IIEF-5 Score | Clinical Classification | |---|---| | 22 to 25 | Normal (no erectile dysfunction) | | 17 to 21 | Mild erectile dysfunction | | 12 to 16 | Mild-to-moderate erectile dysfunction | | 8 to 11 | Moderate erectile dysfunction | | 5 to 7 | Severe erectile dysfunction | Co-morbidities should always be considered when interpreting the IIEF-5 score and selecting a treatment pathway. Step 1: Entry Point — Patient Presents With Symptoms Of ED The algorithm begins when a patient presents with symptoms of erectile dysfunction. The clinician proceeds immediately to a comprehensive structured assessment before any diagnosis or treatment is made. Step 2: Comprehensive Initial Assessment All patients presenting with symptoms of ED must undergo the following assessment as a combined package: - A comprehensive history including medical history (e.g. cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, neurological conditions), psychological history (e.g. depression, anxiety, relationship difficulties), and sexual history. Partner involvement in history-taking is preferred. - Administration of the IIEF-5 questionnaire to quantify severity and guide treatment decisions. - A focused physical examination to identify underlying medical conditions and co-morbid genital disorders. - Laboratory investigations, ordered at clinical discretion (indicated by ± in source algorithm). - Imaging studies, ordered at clinical discretion (indicated by ± in source algorithm). The outcome of this assessment leads to a formal diagnosis of ED. Step 3: Diagnosis Of ED And Classification By Type Following assessment, the clinician classifies the patient's ED into one of the following types. This classification determines which treatment pathway is followed. Organic ED: ED with a physical or medical cause, including vascular (e.g. arterial insufficiency, veno-occlusive disease), hormonal (e.g. hypogonadism), or neurogenic (e.g. spinal cord injury, post-prostatectomy) aetiology. Patients with organic ED proceed to severity assessment (Step 4). Psychogenic ED: ED arising primarily from psychological causes including performance anxiety, depression, relationship conflict, or other psychosocial stressors. Patients with psychogenic ED proceed directly to the Psychogenic ED Treatment Pathway (Step 5C). Mixed ED: Some patients present with a combination of organic and psychogenic factors (mixed ED). For these patients, the clinician should categorise the severity of mixed ED according to IIEF-5 and manage the case following either the organic or psychogenic pathway depending on which aetiology predominates. Step 4: Severity Assessment For Organic ED — Using IIEF-5 For patients diagnosed with Organic ED, the IIEF-5 score is used to stratify severity into two groups, each leading to a distinct treatment pathway. If the IIEF-5 score is between 8 and 21 (Mild or Moderate ED), the patient follows Pathway A. If the IIEF-5 score is between 5 and 7 (Severe ED), the patient follows Pathway B. Step 5: Treatment Pathways Pathway A — Mild Or Moderate Organic ED (IIEF-5 Score 8 to 21) Patients with mild or moderate organic ED are managed initially by the primary team with the following interventions: - Lifestyle modification (e.g. weight loss, smoking cessation, exercise, glycaemic and blood pressure control). - Pharmacotherapy, specifically phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE5i), offered concurrently with lifestyle modifications (indicated by ± in source algorithm, meaning it is offered but not unconditionally mandatory at this stage). If there is no improvement following the above initial management, the patient is referred to a urologist for consideration of mechanical devices (e.g. vacuum erection device, low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy) or surgical intervention (e.g. penile prosthesis implantation). This referral is a definitive next step, not optional, once initial management has failed. Pathway B — Severe Organic ED (IIEF-5 Score 5 to 7) Patients with severe organic ED are referred directly to a urologist. The urologist manages the patient with the following combined interventions: - Lifestyle modification. - Pharmacotherapy (PDE5i), unless contraindicated. - Mechanical devices (e.g. vacuum erection device or shockwave therapy), offered as an adjunct or alternative to pharmacotherapy. - Surgical intervention (e.g. penile prosthesis), considered when other modalities are insufficient or inappropriate. Pathway C — Psychogenic ED Patients with psychogenic ED are managed with: - Lifestyle modification. - Pharmacotherapy (PDE5i), offered at clinical discretion (indicated by ± in source algorithm). - Referral to mental health professionals for formal psychological intervention (e.g. cognitive-behavioural sex therapy, couples therapy). This referral is a core component of management and is not optional in psychogenic ED. Patients with psychogenic ED who do not improve may also be considered for referral to a urologist for mechanical devices or surgical intervention, following the same pathway as those with organic ED who fail initial management. This is indicated by a dashed arrow in the source algorithm, meaning it is a secondary consideration rather than a primary step. Summary Of Relationships — Algorithm 1 - Symptom presentation leads to comprehensive assessment. - Assessment leads to diagnosis and type classification (organic, psychogenic, or mixed). - Organic ED type leads to IIEF-5 severity classification. - Mild/moderate severity (score 8 to 21) leads to lifestyle modification and pharmacotherapy first, then urologist referral if no improvement. - Severe severity (score 5 to 7) leads directly to urologist referral with combined treatment. - Psychogenic ED leads to lifestyle modification, pharmacotherapy at discretion, and mandatory referral to mental health professionals. - Mixed ED follows either organic or psychogenic pathway based on predominant aetiology, using IIEF-5 to stratify severity. ## Algorithm 2: Classification For ED Patients With Cardiovascular Disease Overview: This algorithm classifies patients with confirmed ED and co-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD) into cardiac risk categories, determines the safety of initiating ED treatment (specifically PDE5i), and resolves the presence of nitrate therapy as a critical contraindication decision point. The algorithm is based on the 2nd and 3rd Princeton Consensus on Sexual Dysfunction and Cardiac Risk. If the patient has vasculogenic ED, an ASCVD (Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease) risk score assessment should be performed before entering the main algorithm. Step 1: Entry Point — Patients With Confirmed ED And Cardiovascular Disease The algorithm applies to patients who have already received a confirmed diagnosis of ED and who are known to have cardiovascular disease or are at cardiovascular risk. The purpose of this algorithm is not to diagnose ED, but to determine the safety of treating it. Step 2: Assessment Of Exercise Ability The first clinical action is to assess the patient's exercise ability. Exercise ability is used to guide the physician in estimating the cardiovascular risk associated with sexual activity, and this assessment must be established before the initiation of any ED treatment. Exercise ability is benchmarked against the metabolic equivalent of sexual activity, which is equivalent to: - Walking 1.6 kilometres (1 mile) on a flat surface in 20 minutes, OR - Briskly climbing two flights of stairs in 10 seconds. The outcome of the exercise ability assessment, combined with the patient's cardiac history, informs the cardiac risk stratification in the next step. Step 3: Cardiac Risk Stratification According To Princeton Consensus Using the patient's cardiovascular history and exercise ability, the clinician stratifies the patient into one of three cardiac risk categories according to the 2nd and 3rd Princeton Consensus. Refer to Table 1 (Princeton Consensus Risk Classification Table) for the specific criteria defining each risk tier. The three risk categories are: Low Risk, Intermediate Risk, and High Risk. Each category leads to a distinct management pathway. Step 4: Risk-Based Management Pathways Low Risk Pathway: Patients classified as Low Risk by the Princeton Consensus stratification may be offered elective (i.e. optional) additional risk assessment at the physician's discretion. This is not a mandatory step. Low-risk patients are managed for their ED by the primary care team. They proceed directly to the Nitrate Assessment (Step 5) to determine which ED treatment is safe to prescribe. Intermediate Risk Pathway: Patients classified as Intermediate Risk must undergo a formal stress test before any ED treatment is initiated. The stress test used is the Bruce treadmill protocol. Sexual activity is considered equivalent to 4 minutes of this protocol. A Pass result is defined as completion of the test without development of symptoms, arrhythmias, or a fall in systolic blood pressure. If the stress test result is a Pass, the patient is reclassified as Low Risk. They are then managed by the primary care team and proceed to the Nitrate Assessment (Step 5). If the stress test result is a Fail, the patient is reclassified as High Risk. They are then referred for further cardiac assessment and ED treatment is deferred until the cardiac condition is stabilised. High Risk Pathway: Patients classified as High Risk — either directly from the Princeton Consensus stratification or following a failed stress test — are referred for further cardiac assessment. ED treatment is deferred and must not be initiated until the underlying cardiac condition has been stabilised and the patient has been re-evaluated. Step 5: Nitrate And Riociguat Assessment — Determining ED Treatment Selection This step applies only to patients who have been cleared for ED treatment (i.e. Low Risk patients, or Intermediate Risk patients who passed the stress test). The critical question at this stage is whether the patient is currently prescribed nitrates or riociguat, as these agents are absolutely contraindicated with PDE5i due to the risk of severe hypotension. Decision Branch A — Patient Is Not Prescribed Nitrates Or Riociguat If the patient is NOT currently prescribed nitrates or riociguat, PDE5i (phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors) therapy is the recommended first-line ED treatment. The clinician selects the appropriate PDE5i agent and dose based on the patient's profile (refer to the pharmacological treatment table in Appendix 6B). Decision Branch B — Patient Is Currently Prescribed Nitrates Or Riociguat If the patient IS currently prescribed nitrates or riociguat, a second-level clinical decision is required: Is the nitrate (or riociguat) therapy essential for the patient's ongoing cardiovascular management? If the nitrate is essential and cannot be safely discontinued, the patient must receive Non-PDE5i treatment for their ED. PDE5i agents are absolutely contraindicated in this scenario. If the nitrate is not essential and can be safely discontinued, the clinician should consider stopping the nitrate therapy, and then — after an appropriate washout period — initiate PDE5i therapy for ED. Summary Of Relationships — Algorithm 2 - Confirmed ED with CVD leads to exercise ability assessment, which informs cardiac risk stratification. - Vasculogenic ED additionally requires ASCVD risk score assessment before risk stratification. - Princeton Consensus stratification classifies the patient as Low Risk, Intermediate Risk, or High Risk. - Low Risk leads directly to nitrate assessment and ED treatment selection by the primary team. - Intermediate Risk leads to a mandatory stress test. A passing result reclassifies the patient as Low Risk (proceed to treatment). A failing result reclassifies the patient as High Risk (defer treatment). - High Risk leads to further cardiac assessment. ED treatment is deferred until cardiac condition is stabilised. - For patients cleared for treatment, if NOT on nitrates/riociguat, the treatment is PDE5i. - For patients cleared for treatment, if ON nitrates/riociguat, the clinician assesses if nitrate is essential. If essential, Non-PDE5i treatment is used. If not essential, nitrate cessation followed by PDE5i is considered. ## Appendix 1: Example Of Search Strategy Clinical Question: What are the safe and effective pharmacological treatments in ED? * phosphodiesterase-5-inhibitors 1. ## Algorithm 2: Classification For ED Patients With Cardiovascular Disease
Overview: This algorithm classifies patients with confirmed ED and co-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD) into cardiac risk categories, determines the safety of initiating ED treatment (specifically PDE5i), and resolves the presence of nitrate therapy as a critical contraindication decision point. The algorithm is based on the 2nd and 3rd Princeton Consensus on Sexual Dysfunction and Cardiac Risk.
If the patient has vasculogenic ED, an ASCVD (Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease) risk score assessment should be performed before entering the main algorithm.
Step 1: Entry Point — Patients With Confirmed ED And Cardiovascular Disease
The algorithm applies to patients who have already received a confirmed diagnosis of ED and who are known to have cardiovascular disease or are at cardiovascular risk. The purpose of this algorithm is not to diagnose ED, but to determine the safety of treating it.
Step 2: Assessment Of Exercise Ability
The first clinical action is to assess the patient's exercise ability. Exercise ability is used to guide the physician in estimating the cardiovascular risk associated with sexual activity, and this assessment must be established before the initiation of any ED treatment.
Exercise ability is benchmarked against the metabolic equivalent of sexual activity, which is equivalent to:
- Walking 1.6 kilometres (1 mile) on a flat surface in 20 minutes, OR
- Briskly climbing two flights of stairs in 10 seconds.
The outcome of the exercise ability assessment, combined with the patient's cardiac history, informs the cardiac risk stratification in the next step.
Step 3: Cardiac Risk Stratification According To Princeton Consensus
Using the patient's cardiovascular history and exercise ability, the clinician stratifies the patient into one of three cardiac risk categories according to the 2nd and 3rd Princeton Consensus. Refer to Table 1 (Princeton Consensus Risk Classification Table) for the specific criteria defining each risk tier.
The three risk categories are: Low Risk, Intermediate Risk, and High Risk. Each category leads to a distinct management pathway.
Step 4: Risk-Based Management Pathways
Low Risk Pathway:
Patients classified as Low Risk by the Princeton Consensus stratification may be offered elective (i.e. optional) additional risk assessment at the physician's discretion. This is not a mandatory step.
Low-risk patients are managed for their ED by the primary care team. They proceed directly to the Nitrate Assessment (Step 5) to determine which ED treatment is safe to prescribe.
Intermediate Risk Pathway:
Patients classified as Intermediate Risk must undergo a formal stress test before any ED treatment is initiated.
The stress test used is the Bruce treadmill protocol. Sexual activity is considered equivalent to 4 minutes of this protocol. A Pass result is defined as completion of the test without development of symptoms, arrhythmias, or a fall in systolic blood pressure.
If the stress test result is a Pass, the patient is reclassified as Low Risk. They are then managed by the primary care team and proceed to the Nitrate Assessment (Step 5).
If the stress test result is a Fail, the patient is reclassified as High Risk. They are then referred for further cardiac assessment and ED treatment is deferred until the cardiac condition is stabilised.
High Risk Pathway:
Patients classified as High Risk — either directly from the Princeton Consensus stratification or following a failed stress test — are referred for further cardiac assessment. ED treatment is deferred and must not be initiated until the underlying cardiac condition has been stabilised and the patient has been re-evaluated.
Step 5: Nitrate And Riociguat Assessment — Determining ED Treatment Selection
This step applies only to patients who have been cleared for ED treatment (i.e. Low Risk patients, or Intermediate Risk patients who passed the stress test). The critical question at this stage is whether the patient is currently prescribed nitrates or riociguat, as these agents are absolutely contraindicated with PDE5i due to the risk of severe hypotension.
Decision Branch A — Patient Is Not Prescribed Nitrates Or Riociguat
If the patient is NOT currently prescribed nitrates or riociguat, PDE5i (phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors) therapy is the recommended first-line ED treatment. The clinician selects the appropriate PDE5i agent and dose based on the patient's profile (refer to the pharmacological treatment table in Appendix 6B).
Decision Branch B — Patient Is Currently Prescribed Nitrates Or Riociguat
If the patient IS currently prescribed nitrates or riociguat, a second-level clinical decision is required: Is the nitrate (or riociguat) therapy essential for the patient's ongoing cardiovascular management?
If the nitrate is essential and cannot be safely discontinued, the patient must receive Non-PDE5i treatment for their ED. PDE5i agents are absolutely contraindicated in this scenario.
If the nitrate is not essential and can be safely discontinued, the clinician should consider stopping the nitrate therapy, and then — after an appropriate washout period — initiate PDE5i therapy for ED.
Summary Of Relationships — Algorithm 2
- Confirmed ED with CVD leads to exercise ability assessment, which informs cardiac risk stratification.
- Vasculogenic ED additionally requires ASCVD risk score assessment before risk stratification.
- Princeton Consensus stratification classifies the patient as Low Risk, Intermediate Risk, or High Risk.
- Low Risk leads directly to nitrate assessment and ED treatment selection by the primary team.
- Intermediate Risk leads to a mandatory stress test. A passing result reclassifies the patient as Low Risk (proceed to treatment). A failing result reclassifies the patient as High Risk (defer treatment).
- High Risk leads to further cardiac assessment. ED treatment is deferred until cardiac condition is stabilised.
- For patients cleared for treatment, if NOT on nitrates/riociguat, the treatment is PDE5i.
- For patients cleared for treatment, if ON nitrates/riociguat, the clinician assesses if nitrate is essential. If essential, Non-PDE5i treatment is used. If not essential, nitrate cessation followed by PDE5i is considered.

# Appendix > **Context:** Key Recommendations + reference appendices for the 2024 Malaysian Management of ED CPG. Includes the diagnosis/treatment algorithm, cardiovascular-disease classification (Princeton consensus), history-taking template, IIEF-5 and EHS questionnaires, PDE5i dosing/contraindications, and procedural references (VED, low-intensity shockwave, penile prosthesis). The Key Recommendations are a consolidated digest — full clinical rationale is in Sections 2–8. ## Key Recommendations The following recommendations are highlighted by the CPG DG as the key recommendations that answer the main questions addressed in the CPG and should be prioritised for implementation. Diagnosis And Assessment: * A comprehensive medical, psychosocial and sexual history should be taken in every patient presenting with erectile dysfunction (ED). * A validated questionnaire related to ED should be used to assess all sexual function domains (e.g. International Index of Erectile Function). * A focused physical examination in the initial assessment of men with ED should be done to identify underlying medical conditions and co-morbid genital disorders that may be associated with ED. * Routine laboratory tests should be performed to identify modifiable risk factors of ED. * Patients with ED should have cardiac risk assessment and vice versa. Treatment: * All patients with erectile dysfunction (ED) should be advised on lifestyle and risk factor modifications. * Phosphodiesterase-5-inhibitor should be offered to all patients with ED unless contraindicated. * Mechanical devices (e.g. using vacuum erection device or shockwave therapy) may be offered in ED. Low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy should be performed by urologists for mild to moderate ED. * Penile prothesis may be offered to patients with ED who have failed other interventions. * An integrated and collaborative approach with psychological interventions should be considered in the treatment of ED. ## Algorithm 1: Diagnosis And Treatment Of ED Overview: This algorithm outlines the complete clinical decision pathway for diagnosing and treating Erectile Dysfunction (ED), from initial patient presentation through to specific treatment selection. The pathway branches based on the type of ED identified (organic or psychogenic) and, for organic ED, further branches based on severity as determined by the IIEF-5 score. **Clinical Definitions And Scoring Reference** IIEF-5 (International Index of Erectile Function, 5-item version) is the validated scoring tool used to assess erectile function and classify severity. The total score is the sum of the ordinal responses to all 5 questions (range: 5 to 25). | IIEF-5 Score | Clinical Classification | |---|---| | 22 to 25 | Normal (no erectile dysfunction) | | 17 to 21 | Mild erectile dysfunction | | 12 to 16 | Mild-to-moderate erectile dysfunction | | 8 to 11 | Moderate erectile dysfunction | | 5 to 7 | Severe erectile dysfunction | Co-morbidities should always be considered when interpreting the IIEF-5 score and selecting a treatment pathway. Step 1: Entry Point — Patient Presents With Symptoms Of ED The algorithm begins when a patient presents with symptoms of erectile dysfunction. The clinician proceeds immediately to a comprehensive structured assessment before any diagnosis or treatment is made. Step 2: Comprehensive Initial Assessment All patients presenting with symptoms of ED must undergo the following assessment as a combined package: - A comprehensive history including medical history (e.g. cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, neurological conditions), psychological history (e.g. depression, anxiety, relationship difficulties), and sexual history. Partner involvement in history-taking is preferred. - Administration of the IIEF-5 questionnaire to quantify severity and guide treatment decisions. - A focused physical examination to identify underlying medical conditions and co-morbid genital disorders. - Laboratory investigations, ordered at clinical discretion (indicated by ± in source algorithm). - Imaging studies, ordered at clinical discretion (indicated by ± in source algorithm). The outcome of this assessment leads to a formal diagnosis of ED. Step 3: Diagnosis Of ED And Classification By Type Following assessment, the clinician classifies the patient's ED into one of the following types. This classification determines which treatment pathway is followed. Organic ED: ED with a physical or medical cause, including vascular (e.g. arterial insufficiency, veno-occlusive disease), hormonal (e.g. hypogonadism), or neurogenic (e.g. spinal cord injury, post-prostatectomy) aetiology. Patients with organic ED proceed to severity assessment (Step 4). Psychogenic ED: ED arising primarily from psychological causes including performance anxiety, depression, relationship conflict, or other psychosocial stressors. Patients with psychogenic ED proceed directly to the Psychogenic ED Treatment Pathway (Step 5C). Mixed ED: Some patients present with a combination of organic and psychogenic factors (mixed ED). For these patients, the clinician should categorise the severity of mixed ED according to IIEF-5 and manage the case following either the organic or psychogenic pathway depending on which aetiology predominates. Step 4: Severity Assessment For Organic ED — Using IIEF-5 For patients diagnosed with Organic ED, the IIEF-5 score is used to stratify severity into two groups, each leading to a distinct treatment pathway. If the IIEF-5 score is between 8 and 21 (Mild or Moderate ED), the patient follows Pathway A. If the IIEF-5 score is between 5 and 7 (Severe ED), the patient follows Pathway B. Step 5: Treatment Pathways Pathway A — Mild Or Moderate Organic ED (IIEF-5 Score 8 to 21) Patients with mild or moderate organic ED are managed initially by the primary team with the following interventions: - Lifestyle modification (e.g. weight loss, smoking cessation, exercise, glycaemic and blood pressure control). - Pharmacotherapy, specifically phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE5i), offered concurrently with lifestyle modifications (indicated by ± in source algorithm, meaning it is offered but not unconditionally mandatory at this stage). If there is no improvement following the above initial management, the patient is referred to a urologist for consideration of mechanical devices (e.g. vacuum erection device, low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy) or surgical intervention (e.g. penile prosthesis implantation). This referral is a definitive next step, not optional, once initial management has failed. Pathway B — Severe Organic ED (IIEF-5 Score 5 to 7) Patients with severe organic ED are referred directly to a urologist. The urologist manages the patient with the following combined interventions: - Lifestyle modification. - Pharmacotherapy (PDE5i), unless contraindicated. - Mechanical devices (e.g. vacuum erection device or shockwave therapy), offered as an adjunct or alternative to pharmacotherapy. - Surgical intervention (e.g. penile prosthesis), considered when other modalities are insufficient or inappropriate. Pathway C — Psychogenic ED Patients with psychogenic ED are managed with: - Lifestyle modification. - Pharmacotherapy (PDE5i), offered at clinical discretion (indicated by ± in source algorithm). - Referral to mental health professionals for formal psychological intervention (e.g. cognitive-behavioural sex therapy, couples therapy). This referral is a core component of management and is not optional in psychogenic ED. Patients with psychogenic ED who do not improve may also be considered for referral to a urologist for mechanical devices or surgical intervention, following the same pathway as those with organic ED who fail initial management. This is indicated by a dashed arrow in the source algorithm, meaning it is a secondary consideration rather than a primary step. Summary Of Relationships — Algorithm 1 - Symptom presentation leads to comprehensive assessment. - Assessment leads to diagnosis and type classification (organic, psychogenic, or mixed). - Organic ED type leads to IIEF-5 severity classification. - Mild/moderate severity (score 8 to 21) leads to lifestyle modification and pharmacotherapy first, then urologist referral if no improvement. - Severe severity (score 5 to 7) leads directly to urologist referral with combined treatment. - Psychogenic ED leads to lifestyle modification, pharmacotherapy at discretion, and mandatory referral to mental health professionals. - Mixed ED follows either organic or psychogenic pathway based on predominant aetiology, using IIEF-5 to stratify severity. ## Algorithm 2: Classification For ED Patients With Cardiovascular Disease Overview: This algorithm classifies patients with confirmed ED and co-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD) into cardiac risk categories, determines the safety of initiating ED treatment (specifically PDE5i), and resolves the presence of nitrate therapy as a critical contraindication decision point. The algorithm is based on the 2nd and 3rd Princeton Consensus on Sexual Dysfunction and Cardiac Risk. If the patient has vasculogenic ED, an ASCVD (Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease) risk score assessment should be performed before entering the main algorithm. Step 1: Entry Point — Patients With Confirmed ED And Cardiovascular Disease The algorithm applies to patients who have already received a confirmed diagnosis of ED and who are known to have cardiovascular disease or are at cardiovascular risk. The purpose of this algorithm is not to diagnose ED, but to determine the safety of treating it. Step 2: Assessment Of Exercise Ability The first clinical action is to assess the patient's exercise ability. Exercise ability is used to guide the physician in estimating the cardiovascular risk associated with sexual activity, and this assessment must be established before the initiation of any ED treatment. Exercise ability is benchmarked against the metabolic equivalent of sexual activity, which is equivalent to: - Walking 1.6 kilometres (1 mile) on a flat surface in 20 minutes, OR - Briskly climbing two flights of stairs in 10 seconds. The outcome of the exercise ability assessment, combined with the patient's cardiac history, informs the cardiac risk stratification in the next step. Step 3: Cardiac Risk Stratification According To Princeton Consensus Using the patient's cardiovascular history and exercise ability, the clinician stratifies the patient into one of three cardiac risk categories according to the 2nd and 3rd Princeton Consensus. Refer to Table 1 (Princeton Consensus Risk Classification Table) for the specific criteria defining each risk tier. The three risk categories are: Low Risk, Intermediate Risk, and High Risk. Each category leads to a distinct management pathway. Step 4: Risk-Based Management Pathways Low Risk Pathway: Patients classified as Low Risk by the Princeton Consensus stratification may be offered elective (i.e. optional) additional risk assessment at the physician's discretion. This is not a mandatory step. Low-risk patients are managed for their ED by the primary care team. They proceed directly to the Nitrate Assessment (Step 5) to determine which ED treatment is safe to prescribe. Intermediate Risk Pathway: Patients classified as Intermediate Risk must undergo a formal stress test before any ED treatment is initiated. The stress test used is the Bruce treadmill protocol. Sexual activity is considered equivalent to 4 minutes of this protocol. A Pass result is defined as completion of the test without development of symptoms, arrhythmias, or a fall in systolic blood pressure. If the stress test result is a Pass, the patient is reclassified as Low Risk. They are then managed by the primary care team and proceed to the Nitrate Assessment (Step 5). If the stress test result is a Fail, the patient is reclassified as High Risk. They are then referred for further cardiac assessment and ED treatment is deferred until the cardiac condition is stabilised. High Risk Pathway: Patients classified as High Risk — either directly from the Princeton Consensus stratification or following a failed stress test — are referred for further cardiac assessment. ED treatment is deferred and must not be initiated until the underlying cardiac condition has been stabilised and the patient has been re-evaluated. Step 5: Nitrate And Riociguat Assessment — Determining ED Treatment Selection This step applies only to patients who have been cleared for ED treatment (i.e. Low Risk patients, or Intermediate Risk patients who passed the stress test). The critical question at this stage is whether the patient is currently prescribed nitrates or riociguat, as these agents are absolutely contraindicated with PDE5i due to the risk of severe hypotension. Decision Branch A — Patient Is Not Prescribed Nitrates Or Riociguat If the patient is NOT currently prescribed nitrates or riociguat, PDE5i (phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors) therapy is the recommended first-line ED treatment. The clinician selects the appropriate PDE5i agent and dose based on the patient's profile (refer to the pharmacological treatment table in Appendix 6B). Decision Branch B — Patient Is Currently Prescribed Nitrates Or Riociguat If the patient IS currently prescribed nitrates or riociguat, a second-level clinical decision is required: Is the nitrate (or riociguat) therapy essential for the patient's ongoing cardiovascular management? If the nitrate is essential and cannot be safely discontinued, the patient must receive Non-PDE5i treatment for their ED. PDE5i agents are absolutely contraindicated in this scenario. If the nitrate is not essential and can be safely discontinued, the clinician should consider stopping the nitrate therapy, and then — after an appropriate washout period — initiate PDE5i therapy for ED. Summary Of Relationships — Algorithm 2 - Confirmed ED with CVD leads to exercise ability assessment, which informs cardiac risk stratification. - Vasculogenic ED additionally requires ASCVD risk score assessment before risk stratification. - Princeton Consensus stratification classifies the patient as Low Risk, Intermediate Risk, or High Risk. - Low Risk leads directly to nitrate assessment and ED treatment selection by the primary team. - Intermediate Risk leads to a mandatory stress test. A passing result reclassifies the patient as Low Risk (proceed to treatment). A failing result reclassifies the patient as High Risk (defer treatment). - High Risk leads to further cardiac assessment. ED treatment is deferred until cardiac condition is stabilised. - For patients cleared for treatment, if NOT on nitrates/riociguat, the treatment is PDE5i. - For patients cleared for treatment, if ON nitrates/riociguat, the clinician assesses if nitrate is essential. If essential, Non-PDE5i treatment is used. If not essential, nitrate cessation followed by PDE5i is considered. ## Appendix 1: Example Of Search Strategy Clinical Question: What are the safe and effective pharmacological treatments in ED? * phosphodiesterase-5-inhibitors 1. B) Treatment * What are the safe and effective non-pharmacological treatments in ED? * life-style changes to modify risk factors * smoking * diet * alcohol consumption * obesity * stress * physical activity * metabolic syndrome * device (second stage) * vacuum pump * shockwave therapy * psychosocial/psychopathological treatment * What are the safe and effective pharmacological treatments in ED? * oral medications e.g. phosphodiesterase-5-inhibitors * topical/intraurethral alprostadil (vasoactive agents) * intra-cavernous penile injection with vasoactive agents * What are the safe and effective surgical interventions in ED? * penile prosthesis * surgery for penile revascularisation C) Traditional And Complementary Medicine * What are the safe and effective treatment and complementary medicine (TCM) in ED? D) Follow-Up, Monitoring And Referral * What is the effective follow-up and monitoring schedule for ED? * When should patient with ED be referred for secondary/tertiary care? * urologist * cardiologist * neurologist * endocrinologist * psychiatrist * shared-care concept/multidisciplinary E) Special Groups * What are the safe and effective treatment modalities in ED for the following special groups? * patients with cardiac disease * patients with pelvic surgery or prostate cancer treatment * spinal cord injury survivors ## Appendix 3: Relevant History Taking In Patients With Symptoms Of ED | History Components | Questions | |--------------------|-----------| | History of presenting complaint | Patients with suspected ED will primarily complain of difficulties initiating or sustaining an erection. Further details surrounding these issues should be explored:
• Onset of sexual dysfunction (i.e. acute, gradual)
• Duration of sexual dysfunction
• Lack of libido
• Rigidity of erection
• Duration of sexual stimulation
• Difficulties with ejaculation/orgasm
• Absence of morning erection | | Past medical/ surgical history | Previous sexual dysfunction, CVD, metabolic syndrome (i.e. hypertension, DM, obesity and dyslipidaemia) and pelvic surgery | | Medication history | Antihypertensives, antidepressants, antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, nitrates and PDE5i | | Psychiatric history | Current or previous psychological problems (e.g. depression, anxiety), stress, coping abilities, cognitive factors and previous trauma | | Social history | Smoking, alcohol consumption, illicit drug use, diet, exercise, cultural and religious aspects | | Sexual history | Current sexual partner(s), relationship status, partner's perception to ED, gender dysphoria or sexual orientation, sexual exposure and experience (e.g. masturbation, pornography consumption), plan for children | ## Appendix 4: 5-Item Version Of International Index Of Erectile Function (IIEF-5) A) English Version Patient Name: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Date of Birth: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Date Completed: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Over the past 6 months: | Question | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1. Step 2: Preparation and Vacuum Application * Visual Representation: An illustration shows a patient standing, holding the assembled vacuum chamber over the penis, pressing the open end firmly against the pubic area while operating the pump to create negative pressure. * Description & Procedure: * Before the device is used, the elastic constricting band is lubricated with a water-soluble jelly and placed around the outer rim of the vacuum chamber near its open end. * A generous amount of water-soluble lubricant/jelly is next applied directly to the base of the penis and surrounding pubic area to assure a completely airtight seal when the chamber is pressed against the body. * The penis is carefully placed inside the vacuum chamber, and the pump is operated to create a vacuum. The negative pressure draws blood into the corpora cavernosa. The vacuum is applied for 3 to 6 minutes, or until the penis becomes fully rigid. Step 3: Band Placement and Chamber Removal * Visual Representation: An illustration shows a close-up of the patient's hands sliding the elastic constricting band from the base of the cylinder onto the root of the now-erect penis, followed by releasing the vacuum pressure. * Description & Safety Guidelines: * Once full rigidity is achieved, the elastic constricting band is slid off the end of the vacuum chamber directly onto the base/root of the penis to trap the blood and maintain the erection. * The vacuum release valve on the pump is then pressed to release the pressure, and the chamber is safely removed from the penis. Sexual intercourse can be performed immediately after. * Safety Warning: The constricting band must not be left on the penis for longer than 30 minutes to prevent tissue ischemia and permanent injury. ## Appendix 8: Low-Intensity Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy Anatomical and Treatment Overview * Visual Representation: Illustrations show the anatomy of the penis including the glans penis, corpus cavernosum, corpus spongiosum, bulbospongiosus muscle, and ischiocavernosus muscle. The highlighted treatment area targets the crura and penile shaft. * How it works? * While the patient is lying down, ultrasound gel is applied to the applicator head and/or the treatment area. * The applicator head is applied to areas of the penile shaft and crus. * The shockwave technology skilfully creates waves that treat a broad area from the superficial surface of the penile shaft to the deeper erectile tissues of the crura. * It is currently recommended that this treatment to be conducted once or twice a week, for at least 6 sessions. * The waves stimulate tissue and do not cause any pain or external scarring. Patients can resume daily regular activity after the procedure. ### 8.2.9: Anti-Ischemic — Nitrates
Nitrates are effective in the management of angina due to their coronary arteriolar and venous vasodilatation properties that result in a reduction in preload and afterload.
A) Nitrates for acute angina
Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) can be given for immediate relief of angina. The aerosol formulation has a faster onset of action. GTN improves exercise tolerance when given prophylactically, thus preventing anticipated angina caused by exertion. Besides its anti-anginal properties, GTN also has shown antithrombotic and antiplatelet activity.
GTN tablets should be kept in an amber coloured bottle and protected from sunlight. Once the bottle has been opened, the life-span is reduced to 8 weeks. The aerosol formulation can be used until the expiry date.
B) Nitrates for angina treatment and prophylaxis
Nitrates are often used with β-blockers or CCBs to prevent or reduce angina and increase exercise tolerance in symptomatic patients. Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN) has similar efficacy as isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN) but with a longer duration of action and a better side effect profile.
Long-term regular use of nitrates without a nitrate-free or nitrate-low interval of about 8-10 hours can lead to nitrate tolerance. This could offset the beneficial short-term ischemic preconditioning effects and potentially worsen endothelial dysfunction. Twice daily dosing of ISDN that provides a 10-12-hour nitrate-free interval each day is preferred.
The most common side effect of nitrates is headache. It may also cause hypotension. Concurrent use with a phosphodiesterase type-5 (PDE5) inhibitor like sildenafil is contraindicated because of severe hypotension.

# Section 8: Management ## 8.0: Management of Stable CAD The treatment goals in stable CAD are to: - alleviate symptoms and improve quality of life, - reduce risk of adverse CV outcomes and improve survival and - prevent progression of atherosclerotic disease. Optimal Medical Therapy (OMT) is the cornerstone of management of patients with both obstructive and non-obstructive CAD. It has been shown to improve prognosis, reduce symptoms and myocardial ischemia. [Grade I, Level A] OMT involves: - intensive lifestyle changes (healthy diet, regular physical activity, smoking cessation and optimal management of risk factors and weight) - pharmacotherapy which includes anti-platelet agents and statins to achieve target LDL-C. In addition, ACEi, β-blockers and anti-anginal medications may be necessary to treat co-existing hypertension, LV dysfunction and/or angina. The management of these patients with Stable CAD should be multifaceted and include: - behavioural modification therapy (BMT) - patient education and lifestyle modification - pharmacological therapy - myocardial revascularization when indicated. All patients should be educated on behavioural modification therapy and receive OMT for survival benefit. Treatment of CV risk factors to target and adherence to treatment recommendations should also be addressed. ## 8.1: Behavioural Modification Therapy (BMT) ### 8.1.1: Patient Education - cause of angina and factors that can provoke symptoms. - circumstances in which urgent medical attention should be sought, especially if there is a sudden worsening in symptom frequency or severity. - role and importance of behavioural modification. - risk-benefit profile of pharmacological treatments. - importance of adherence to treatment recommendations and OMT. ### 8.1.2: Diet Dietary habits influence a variety of cardio-metabolic risk factors such as body weight, cholesterol, blood pressure, glucose metabolism, oxidative stress and inflammation. It is being increasingly recognized that instead of focussing on specific nutrients, it is more important to look at specific foods and overall dietary patterns. A Mediterranean diet significantly reduces CV events. The Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet is associated with a significant reduction in hypertension. A ‘high-fat/low-fibre’ and ‘high-sugar’ diet showed a trend for an increased risk of CV events in older men aged 60-79 years. General recommendations should fit in with the local culture. Energy intake should be adjusted to avoid overweight/obesity. (refer to Table 9: Nutritional Recommendations) Refer to CPG Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease 2017. Table 9: Nutritional Recommendations | | Recommended Nutrient Intake; Dietary Patterns | Grade of Recommendation and Level of Evidence | |---|---|---| | **A** | **Fat requirements**

This is equivalent to 50 g (or around 12 level teaspoons) for an adult of healthy body weight consuming approximately 2000 calories per day | [Grade I, Level A] | | | • <5 g salt or 1 level teaspoon per day or (2000 mg sodium per day) | [Grade I, Level A] | | | • Abstinence or not more than 1-2 standard servings of alcohol intake per day. | [Grade II-a, Level B] | *\*In individuals with Very High and High CV risk advise < 200mg cholesterol a day* ### 8.1.3: Physical Activity Any amount of physical activity (PA) is better than none, as it can offer health benefits. As secondary prevention in patients with stable CAD and post ACS, regular PA confers significant mortality and morbidity benefits. Thus it should be incorporated into daily activities. PA is any bodily movement that substantially increases energy expenditure. This includes: (refer to Table 10: Classification Of Physical Activity) - leisure-time physical activities - occupational activities - commuting activities - exercise: a subset of PA that is planned and structured, involving repetitive bodily movement done with a goal to improve or maintain physical fitness. Aerobic exercise should be offered to patients with stable CAD, usually as part of a structured cardiac rehabilitation program. This is a medically supervised program consisting of exercise training, education on heart healthy living and counselling to reduce stress. It helps patients return to an active lifestyle and recover more quickly. In addition, a cardiac rehabilitation program: - helps the identification and management of comorbid conditions and psychosocial disorder (anxiety and depression). - ensures patient adherence to medical and lifestyle therapies to achieve cardiovascular (CVD) prevention goals. [Grade I, Level B] The recommended duration of PA in healthy adults regardless of age is: - at least 150 minutes a week of moderate intensity or - 75 minutes a week of vigorous intensity PA or an equivalent combination [Grade I, Level B] Sedentary patients should be strongly encouraged to start light-intensity exercise programmes after an adequate exercise-related risk stratification. In patients with significant CAD who are not candidates for revascularization, exercise training may offer an alternative means of symptom alleviation and improved prognosis. [Grade I, Level B] All individuals should be encouraged to exercise. Any amount of PA is better than none. Wherever possible, individuals should be referred to physiotherapists/exercise physiologists for exercise prescription. • Stair-treadmill | ### 8.1.4: Smoking Cessation Smoking is an independent risk factor for CVD. It also interacts with other CV risk factors, such as glucose intolerance and low serum levels of HDL-C in a multiplicative manner. Examples: - the presence of smoking alone is reported to double the level of risk, but the simultaneous presence of another major risk factor is estimated to quadruple the risk (2 × 2). - the presence of two other risk factors with smoking may result in approximately eight times the risk (2 × 2 × 2) of persons with no risk factors. [Grade I, Level B] Smoking is an important cause of plaque rupture leading to ACS. Data from the NCVD-ACS Registry 2014-2015 showed that 37% of patients were smokers. In the INTERHEART study, a dose response relationship was demonstrated between the number of cigarettes smoked and MI, where smokers who smoked >40 cig/day were found to have a 9-fold relative risk of MI compared with non-smokers. Changing cigarette designs such as filtered, low-tar, and "light" variations, have not reduced overall disease risk among smokers. Stopping smoking after an MI is the most effective prevention measure. There is significant reduction on morbidity within the first 6 months of quitting and the risks of CVD almost equals the risk of never smokers after 10-15 years of cessation. Patients may be referred to the mQuit Services. Currently this smoking cessation service is being implemented both in government and private facilities including general practice clinics, private hospital and community pharmacies. More information is available at www.jomquit.moh.gov.my Non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke increase their risk of developing: - CHD by 25-30%. - stroke by 20-30%. - lung cancer by 20-30%. There is no safe level of exposure to second-hand tobacco smoke. [Grade III, Level B] E-cigarette aerosol (vaping) is harmful. - The use of products containing nicotine poses dangers to youth, pregnant women, and foetuses. - Nicotine exposure during adolescence can cause addiction and can harm the developing adolescent brain. The use of e-cigarettes and shisha are not recommended. ### 8.1.5: Weight Management Both overweight and obesity are associated with an increased risk of death in CAD. Obesity increases the risk of: - all-cause mortality by about 20%. - overall CV mortality by 50%. - CHD mortality by about 50% in women and about 60% in men. Every 5 kg/m² higher BMI, was associated, on the average, with a 30% higher overall mortality and 40% increase for vascular mortality. In morbid obesity (BMI ≥40 kg/m²) CV mortality is increased by 200% to 300%. The presence of sleep apnoea symptoms should be carefully assessed, especially in obese patients. Sleep apnoea has been associated with an increase in CV mortality and morbidity. Weight loss is a challenge and preventing weight regain after weight loss may be even more difficult. Modest weight loss of between 5 to 10%, can reduce blood pressure (BP), improve glycaemic control, lipid profile, and quality of life. [Grade I, Level B] The goals of weight management are to achieve 5 to 10% weight loss and to maintain this over a period of 1-2 years before attempting further weight loss. Methods of weight loss include dietary intervention, increased physical activity, behavioural modifications (e.g. self-monitoring of eating habits), pharmacological agents and bariatric surgery. Anti-obesity drugs that are available locally are: - Sympathomimetic (Phentermine) - this drug should not be used continuously for longer than 6 months at any one time. - Lipase Inhibitor - Orlistat. - Glucagon-like peptide 1 Receptor Agonist - Liraglutide. [Grade II-a, Level B] These drugs may be considered for overweight and obese people with: - BMI >25.0 kg/m² plus 2 CV risk factors or - BMI ≥27.0 kg/m² after failing to lose weight despite 6 months of lifestyle modification [Grade II-a, Level B] In patients with morbid obesity, bariatric surgery may be considered. [… 8.2: Pharmacological Therapy shown above …] receptor-neprilysin inhibitors may also be considered. - Optimal medical therapy should be instituted prior to revascularization procedures. ## 8.3: Myocardial Revascularization Recent clinical trials have not shown that an initial strategy of PCI in combination with OMT to be superior to OMT alone in reducing death, MI or repeat revascularization during short term and long term follow up. In a small randomised controlled trial, PCI did not improve exercise time or angina frequency at 6 weeks when compared to a sham procedure. CABG however, has been shown to improve survival when compared to OMT in patients with LM or three-vessel stable CAD, particularly when the proximal LAD is involved. Benefits are greater in those with severe symptoms, early positive exercise tests, and impaired LV function. The decision to revascularize patients with stable CAD on OMT will depend on: - [Grade I, Level C] Symptoms - presence of angina affecting quality of life - [Grade II-a, Level B] Extent of ischemia as determined by non-invasive testing - mild vs moderate to severe myocardial ischemia. Individuals with moderate to severe ischemia benefit from revascularization while those with no or mild ischemia do better with OMT (Refer to Table 2: Prognostic Indicators For Adverse CV Outcomes On Non-Invasive Testing) - [Grade I, Level A] Extent and severity of coronary disease and where applicable physiological functional testing using FFR: - FFR <0.75 - benefit from revascularisation as compared to OMT. - FFR between >0.75 but <0.8 - have intermediate benefit with revascularisation and management should be based on clinical judgement. - FFR >0.8 - no benefit from revascularisation. Revascularization has generally been shown to be more effective than OMT in relieving angina and myocardial ischemia. Choice of revascularization strategies is guided by several factors such as number of coronary vessels involved, anatomic complexity of the target lesions, likelihood of complete revascularization, patient comorbidities as well as preference (Refer to Table 12: Factors Influencing Decision On Revascularization Strategies). Table 12: Factors Influencing Decision On Revascularization Strategies | Factors | Description | |---|---| | Anatomical Factors | Single versus multivessel disease, left main involvement, proximal LAD, chronic total occlusion, number of patent coronaries and SYNTAX score | | Technical Factors | Lesion length, calcification, tortuosity, aneurysms, previous PCI or CABG, complete versus incomplete revascularization | | Patient Factors | Age, gender, presence of comorbidities such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease, fragility, previous stroke, peripheral artery disease, bleeding risk and life expectancy | | Other Factors | Cost, availability of expertise, experience of the operator, patient's preference, volume of the centre and waiting list | There is an inherent difference between the 2 modes of myocardial revascularisation - PCI treats only the coronary lesion and leaves the other segments alone while CABG treats the entire vessel proximal to the site of implantation of the graft. Wherever possible, a discussion with the patient and Heart Team should be encouraged prior to revascularization. In general, in patients with a low burden of CAD - single vessel disease not involving proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD) or dominant circumflex artery, low-risk findings on non-invasive testing and absence of LV systolic dysfunction and diabetes, OMT should be the initial step. In the presence of continuing symptoms and impaired quality of life, PCI may be an option if the coronary stenosis is significant (FFR <0.8). In patients with complex CAD, evaluation by a Heart Team is recommended. For patients with multivessel CAD, preserved LV systolic function, low complexity coronary anatomy, and absence of diabetes, PCI may be considered. In patients with multivessel disease, complex anatomy, diabetes and low surgical risk, CABG has a better survival benefit. Please refer to Malaysian Appropriate Use Criteria for Investigations and Revascularizations in CAD, 1st Ed, 2015. Key Messages: The decision to revascularize patients with stable CAD on OMT will depend on: - Symptoms - presence of angina affecting quality of life. - Extent of ischemia as determined by non-invasive testing - mild vs moderate to severe myocardial ischemia. Individuals with moderate to severe ischemia benefit from revascularization while those with no or mild ischemia do better with OMT. (Refer to Table 2: Prognostic Indicators For Adverse CV Outcomes On Non-Invasive Testing) - Extent of coronary disease and where applicable physiological functional testing using FFR. In individuals with: - FFR <0.75 - benefit from revascularisation as compared to OMT. - FFR between >0.75 but <0.8 - have intermediate benefit with revascularisation and management should be based on clinical judgement. - FFR >0.8 - no benefit from revascularisation Wherever possible, a discussion with the patient and Heart Team should be encouraged prior to revascularization to determine the best strategy - PCI or CABG. Recommendation: - The decision to revascularize patients with stable CAD on OMT will depend on: - Symptoms [Grade I, Level C] - Extent of ischemia [Grade II-a, Level B] - Extent of coronary disease and where applicable physiological functional testing using FFR.
